chapter_theme: A bitterly ironic portrait of the base: they look perfectly human, are as free as gods, and are happier than the good because nothing troubles them. Only fear and greed move them, and at the first trouble they sell themselves. The chapter ends the whole Book of Wealth.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: excess of their fault (1071), fearless of blame (1072), do as they please (1073), fault of pride in low conduct (1074), their conduct is not natural to them (1075), can't keep a secret (1076), how they give (1077-1078), envy (1079), and they become slaves (1080). Manakkudavar's text marks 1080 as the end of the Book of Wealth.

1071.reading: The base look just like human beings; we have never seen so close a resemblance.
1071.nuance: Bitter praise opens the portrait. The likeness is complete, and that is the whole problem, since there's no outward way of telling.

positions.position: It is a likeness of body between two different kinds, distinguished only by whether they have good qualities.
It is hypocrisy within one person, who is base while acting good.

1072.reading: The base are more fortunate than those who know what's good, for they have no anguish in their heart.
1072.nuance: A real observation under the sarcasm: moral knowledge has a psychological cost. Parimelazhagar spells it out: the good worry that they don't do enough, about obstacles to their good deeds, and about what might result. திரு here is mock praise, as he says.

1073.reading: The base are like the gods, for they too act as they please.
1073.nuance: Having looked like humans in 1071, they now look like gods. Parimelazhagar says the difference between them goes unstated, since the gods act by understanding and the base by lowness. Kalaignar's gloss says 'the gods of the Puranas', which gives the barb a second target.

1074.reading: Seeing அகப்பட்டி, the base outdo them and swagger with pride.
1074.nuance: அகப்பட்டி is hard to fix, and I've left it untranslated. The readings below differ so widely that I can't be confident of either.

positions.position: These are people who behave as they please like strays, on a smaller scale than the base man, and he boasts by exceeding them.
These are women at home with grace, and the base pride themselves on being more graceful still.

1075.reading: Fear is the conduct of the base, and beyond that there's some, if there's desire.
1075.nuance: A theory of external motivation: there's no inner source of good conduct in them, so it can only come from fear of punishment and hope of gain. Parimelazhagar names the king as what they fear, and Kalaignar reverses the order and makes it pretence.

1076.reading: The base are like a beaten drum, for they carry any secret they hear and proclaim it to others.
1076.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes that the drum only sounds when beaten, a working likeness. உய்த்து, 'carrying', suggests to him the secret is a heavy burden to such a man, so that he has to go and put it down.

1077.reading: The base won't even shake their wet hands for any but those with bent fists who would break their jaws.
1077.nuance: The smallest gift is shaking drops of water off a washed hand. The gift is measured by what it takes to get it. Parimelazhagar sums up: they give nothing to the weak and everything to those who hurt them.

1078.reading: The worthy are of use at a word, and the base, like sugar-cane, only when crushed.
1078.nuance: A sugar-cane is sweet, so the image concedes that the base do have something to give. But it comes out only under pressure. கொல்ல, 'to kill', is unusually strong.

1079.reading: If they see others clothed and fed, the base are able to find a fault in them.
1079.nuance: Ordinary eating and dressing are enough to bring it on; no great success is required.

positions.position: They invent faults that don't exist, with skill enough to make them believable.
They search out faults that do exist in such people.
positions.quote: அவர் மாட்டு உள்ள குற்றங்களை ஆராயவல்லாராவர் கயவர்

1080.reading: What are the base fit for? When something befalls them, they are fit to sell themselves, quickly.
1080.nuance: The Book of Wealth closes with a person as a thing sold. Parimelazhagar's reading of விரைந்து is grim: they hurry before buyers learn what they are. An answer to the question is the insult: this is the only use they have.

links.note: Two responses to the same crisis mark the moral range of the Book of Wealth. When honour or distress comes, those like the yak give up life (969), and the base sell theirs for a price, in haste (1080). The book ends on the second.

A scale of giving. In Parimelazhagar's reading of 1051 the worthiest give before anything is said, in 1078 the worthy give when told, and the base give when crushed. 1077 adds that the base give nothing to any who can't hurt them.
A spy in 587 hears the hidden and knows it without doubt, and in 1076 the base also hear it, but proclaim it. Trading in secrets is a skill or a vice according to whether one can hold them.

368 says there's no suffering for those without desire, the ascetic's freedom from anguish. 1072's base have that freedom, by not knowing what is good. The verse exposes a counterfeit of equanimity: peace of mind can't itself be the measure.

1018 sees shame as the condition of virtue, with virtue itself ashamed to approach the shameless. 1075 is a kind of counter-case: the base still have conduct, with fear and desire in place of shame. Their conduct looks alike and differs in its source.
The same satirical move rises in rank: they're like men, and then they're like gods. What makes them like the gods, acting as they please, is what makes them not like men.

source_issues: 1075: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
1077: Manakkudavar's text ends with a stray digit 8.
1078: Parimelazhagar's gloss has மறைக் கீழாயினார், which seems garbled; and Pope's gloss adds 'bestow their alms', which is not in the Tamil.
1080: Manakkudavar's text ends with colophons for குடியியல் and பொருட்பால், which aren't commentary on this verse.
